cards.q: What is the operational definition of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT)?
cards.a: The intermittent inhalation of **100% oxygen** at pressures greater than **1 atmosphere absolute (ATA)** within a **sealed chamber**.

cards.q: Which physical gas law explains the mechanism of dissolved oxygen elevation in HBOT, and by what factor does it increase at therapeutic pressures?
cards.a: Governed by **Henry's Law**, breathing 100% oxygen at **2.0–3.0 ATA** increases dissolved plasma oxygen by approximately **10–15 fold**, delivering supraphysiological oxygen independent of **hemoglobin concentration**.

cards.q: How does HBOT reduce post-traumatic tissue edema without inducing tissue hypoxia?
cards.a: Hyperoxia induces **vasoconstriction**, which decreases tissue edema in crush injuries, burns, and compartment syndromes, while the marked increase in **dissolved plasma oxygen** prevents tissue hypoxia.

cards.q: What essential cellular repair processes are stimulated by elevated arterial and tissue PO2 during HBOT?
cards.a: Restores aerobic metabolism and accelerates oxygen-dependent processes including **phagocytosis**, **collagen synthesis**, and **angiogenesis**.

cards.q: How does HBOT stimulate angiogenesis across the wound bed?
cards.a: It increases the **oxygen gradient** between the **ischemic center** and the **well-perfused periphery** of the wound.

cards.q: What immunomodulatory and antimicrobial effects does HBOT exert on healing tissues?
cards.a: Shifts macrophages toward **pro-repair phenotypes**, enhances **neutrophil oxidative burst**, suppresses **anaerobic bacterial growth and toxin production**, and potentiates **aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones**.

cards.q: What are standard clinical dosage parameters for HBOT in wound-healing protocols?
cards.a: Pressures of **2.0–2.5 ATA** (up to 3.0 ATA) applied for **60–90 minutes per session**, administered **once or twice daily**.

cards.q: What is the single absolute contraindication to Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) and why?
cards.a: **Untreated pneumothorax**, because pressure changes during compression and decompression can precipitate a **fatal tension pneumothorax** and **gas embolism**.

cards.q: What are the common relative contraindications to HBOT?
cards.a: Includes **claustrophobia**, **asthma**, **COPD**, **pregnancy**, **congenital spherocytosis**, **upper respiratory tract infection**, **fever**, **pacemakers**, and **seizure disorders/epilepsy**.

cards.q: What are the physical characteristics and wavelength spectrum of Polarized Light Therapy (PLT)?
cards.a: It is **polarized**, **polychromatic**, **non-coherent**, and **low-energy** light spanning a spectrum of **480–3400 nm**.

cards.q: What biological effects does Polarized Light Therapy exert during the inflammatory phase of wound healing?
cards.a: Promotes **lymphocyte and monocyte proliferation**, enhances **macrophage and neutrophil counts**, increases **phagocytosis**, downregulates **pro-inflammatory cytokines**, and releases **pro-proliferative growth factors**.

cards.q: How does Polarized Light Therapy influence the proliferative and remodeling phases of wound healing?
cards.a: Stimulates **endothelial growth factors (neovascularization)**, promotes **keratinocyte/fibroblast proliferation**, balances **collagen synthesis with collagenase lysis**, and increases **wound tensile strength**.

cards.q: What are the application distance and angle recommendations for Polarized Light Therapy?
cards.a: The device must be held at a **right angle (perpendicular)** to the wound surface at a fixed distance of **10 cm** after cleansing with saline and betadine.

cards.q: What tissue depths are targeted by specific wavelengths in Polarized Light Therapy?
cards.a: **Red light (630–660 nm)** targets **superficial tissue layers**, whereas **near-infrared light (810–850 nm)** penetrates into **deeper tissues**.

cards.q: What are the recommended dosimetry parameters (energy density and duration) for Polarized Light Therapy?
cards.a: Energy density of **2–10 J/cm²** (typically **2.4 J/cm²** per session) for **5–20 minutes** per wound area.

cards.q: What is the recommended treatment frequency and course duration for Polarized Light Therapy?
cards.a: **3 times per week** for chronic wounds (daily for the first **7–10 days** in acute wounds) until wound closure, extending **2–4 weeks post-closure** for scar remodeling.

cards.q: What are the key contraindications and precautions for Polarized Light Therapy?
cards.a: Direct irradiation over **known malignancies**, **active hemorrhage**, the **thyroid gland**, and the **eyes** (protective eyewear required); caution in **pregnancy** and **photosensitivity**.

cards.q: What is High Voltage Pulsed Current (HVPC) and what is its primary biological mechanism in tissue repair?
cards.a: A **monophasic, twin-peak pulsed direct current** modality that accelerates repair via **galvanotaxis (electrotaxis)** by directing charged cellular migration.

cards.q: What waveform properties allow HVPC to penetrate deep tissues without activating nociceptors?
cards.a: A combination of **high peak voltage (150–500 V)** and an **ultra-short pulse duration (50–100 µs)** that remains below the **chronaxie of pain-mediating A-delta and C fibers**.

cards.q: What are the standard waveform characteristics (phase configuration, frequency, and duty cycle) of HVPC?
cards.a: **Twin-spike monophasic** pulsed DC, frequency of **1–120 pulses per second (PPS)**, and a **duty cycle <1%**, preventing significant thermal tissue injury.

cards.q: What endogenous electrical phenomenon does HVPC mimic in injured skin?
cards.a: Replicates the **transepithelial potential (TEP)** and injury-induced **lateral electric fields of 100–200 mV/mm**, guiding bioelectric cellular healing.

cards.q: When is anodal (+) stimulation indicated over a wound in HVPC, and which cells are recruited?
cards.a: Indicated during the **inflammatory phase**; attracts negatively charged **macrophages (−)** and **neutrophils (−)** to promote **phagocytosis and autolysis**.

cards.q: When is cathodal (−) stimulation indicated over a wound in HVPC, and which cells are recruited?
cards.a: Indicated during the **proliferative and remodeling phases**; attracts positively charged **fibroblasts (+)**, **keratinocytes (+)**, and **epidermal cells (+)** to promote **collagen synthesis and epithelialization**.

cards.q: How should electrodes be sized and configured during HVPC application?
cards.a: The active electrode matches **wound dimensions** (soaked in antiseptic and placed over saline-soaked gauze), while the dispersive electrode is placed **10–20 cm proximal** and sized **2–4× larger** to reduce current density.

cards.q: What are the standard clinical treatment settings (voltage, frequency, time) for HVPC wound healing?
cards.a: Voltage adjusted between **150–350 V**, frequency at **50–100 PPS**, and a duration of **30–60 minutes per session**.

cards.q: What are the four absolute contraindications to the use of HVPC?
cards.a: **Osteomyelitis** (risk of disseminating infection), **active malignancy** (risk of galvanotactic metastasis), **electronic implants (pacemakers/ICDs/pumps)**, and application over the **pregnant uterus/pelvis/lumbar spine**.

cards.q: Why is the anterior cervical region contraindicated for HVPC electrode placement?
cards.a: Stimulation of the **carotid sinus** can precipitate profound **bradycardia**, **hypotension**, and **syncope**.

cards.q: What anatomical regions represent relative contraindications or precautions for HVPC?
cards.a: The **thoracic region** (arrhythmia risk crossing the heart), **cranial region** (cerebral perfusion/ICP shifts), areas of **active hemorrhage**, and areas with **deep vein thrombosis or thrombophlebitis**.

cards.q: What adverse effects can occur from improper application of HVPC?
cards.a: **Skin irritation or chemical burns** (excessive current density or poor contact), **muscle twitching/spasms** (motor nerve activation), and **increased pain**.
